'''Kew Gardens Hills''' is a neighborhood in the middle of the [[New York City]] borough of [[Queens]]. The borders are [[Flushing Meadows–Corona Park]] to the west, the [[Long Island Expressway]] to the north, [[Interstate 495 (New York)|Union Turnpike]] to the south, and Kissena/Parsons Boulevards to the east.

The neighborhood is located near several highways including the Long Island Expressway, [[Grand Central Parkway]], [[Interstate 678|Van Wyck Expressway]], and the [[Jackie Robinson Parkway]] (Interborough). It is also served by several bus routes. Adjacent neighborhoods include [[Forest Hills, Queens|Forest Hills]] to the west, [[Pomonok, Queens|Pomonok]] and [[Hillcrest, Queens|Hillcrest]] to both the east and southeast, [[Briarwood, Queens|Briarwood]] to the south, and [[Queensboro Hill, Queens|Queensboro Hill]] to the north.

Kew Gardens Hills is located in [[Queens Community Board 8|Queens Community District 8]] and its ZIP Code is 11367.<ref name="NYCPlanning"/> It is patrolled by the [[New York City Police Department]]'s 107th Precinct.<ref name="NYPD 107th Precinct"/> Politically, Kew Gardens Hills is represented by the [[New York City Council]]'s 24th District.<ref>[http://www.nyc.gov/html/dc/downloads/pdf/queens.pdf Current City Council Districts for Queens County], [[New York City]]. Accessed May 5, 2017.</ref>

==Geography==
Kew Gardens Hills is situated in the southwestern corner of the area historically known as [[Flushing, Queens#Nineteenth century|the Town of Flushing]], in its 6th district.

As neighborhoods in the City of New York are not designated by the city,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/site/planning/data-maps/city-neighborhoods.page |title=NYC Department of City Planning|publisher=Nyc.gov|access-date=July 26, 2018}}</ref> there are multiple means to determine the geographical boundaries of the area:
*'''General borders:''' The western boundary of the neighborhood is considered to be [[Flushing Meadows–Corona Park]], which is separated from the neighborhood by the [[Interstate 678|Van Wyck Expressway]]. The southern playground of the park however is east of the [[Interstate 678|Van Wyck Expressway]], and is only accessible via an entrance along Park Drive East. Though part of the park, the playground is considered within Kew Gardens Hills. Prior to the building of the [[Interstate 678|Van Wyck Expressway]], the [[IND World's Fair Line]] ran along this route during the [[1939 New York World's Fair]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nycsubway.org/perl/caption.pl?/img/maps/system_1939.jpg|title=1939 Subway Map|publisher=NYCSubway.org|access-date=November 6, 2014}}</ref>
*'''Postal boundaries:''' Since 2003, when the United States Postal Services renamed the post office in [[ZIP Code]] 11367 to the "Kew Gardens Hills Post Office",<ref name="postoffice">{{cite web|url=http://www.timesledger.com/stories/2003/26/20030626-archive94.html |title=Post office on Main Street renamed for neighborhood|publisher=Times Ledger|date=June 26, 2003|access-date=May 11, 2012}}</ref> the borders of the area for ZIP Code purposes extend from the south at [[Union Turnpike (New York)|Union Turnpike]], to the north at the [[Horace Harding Expressway]] and east to [[Parsons Boulevard]].<ref name="usps">{{cite web|url=http://www.usps.com|title=United States Postal Service|publisher=Usps.com|access-date=November 6, 2014}}</ref> Prior to 2003 this Post office was called the Station C Post Office.<ref name=postoffice  /> Although the post office is named "Kew Gardens Hills", the USPS still designates the city or town for purposes of addressing as "Flushing".<ref name=usps />[[File:KewGardensHills_EruvBoundary.jpg|thumb|upright|Boundary sign located over Flushing Meadows-Corona Park demarcating an Eruv boundary of Kew Gardens Hills]]
*'''Other designations:''' Some areas, east of Parsons Boulevard and west of 164th Street, as well as south of Union Turnpike and north of the Grand Central Parkway are included in Kew Gardens Hills, by the NYC Department of Education,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://schools.nyc.gov/schoolsearch/Maps.aspx?grade=ALL&borough=ALL&q=Townsend%20Harris%20High%20School%20%28Q525%29|title=NYC DOE Neighborhood Search|publisher=NYCDOE|access-date=November 6, 2014}}</ref> historians,<ref>[http://forgotten-ny.com/2008/11/kew-gardens-hills-queens/ "Kew Gardens Hills, Queens"], [[Forgotten NY]]. Kevin J. Walsh. Retrieved November 6, 2014.</ref> the Kew Gardens Hills [[Eruv]] Committee, by residents or businesses themselves,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://kewmotorinn.com/ |title=Kew Motor Inn|publisher=Kew Motoe Inn|access-date=November 6, 2014}}</ref> or by real estate brokers.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nybits.com/queens/kew_gardens_hills/|title=Kew Gardens Hills|publisher=NY Bits|access-date=November 6, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hotelplanner.com/Hotels/28167-NEAR-Pomonok|title=Hotels Near Pomonok|publisher=Hotelplanner.com|access-date=November 6, 2014}}</ref>{{paragraph}}In these extended areas—with the exception of some zig-zag borders—residents north of 73rd Avenue use ZIP 11365, south of 73rd Avenue, ZIP 11366, and south of Union Turnpike, ZIPs 11432 and 11435.<ref name="usps"/> These areas include the [[Pomonok, Queens|Pomonok]], [[Electchester, Queens|Electchester]], and [[Parkway Village (Queens)|Parkway Village]] developments, among others. Despite the ZIP Codes with the first three digits as "114" being originally designated in the postal city of "Jamaica", these areas of Kew Gardens Hills are within the geographical limits of the original Town of Flushing.<ref name="Beers 1873 Map">{{cite web|url=http://www.davidrumsey.com/luna/servlet/detail/RUMSEY~8~1~217416~5503590:Flushing,-Queens-Co-,-L-I---insets-?sort=Pub_List_No_InitialSort%2CPub_Date%2CPub_List_No%2CSeries_No&qvq=w4s:/who/Beers,%20F.W./what/County%20Atlas/where/Flushing%20%28N.Y.%29/when/1873;sort:Pub_List_No_InitialSort%2CPub_Date%2CPub_List_No%2CSeries_No;lc:RUMSEY~8~1&mi=0&trs=9 |title=Beers 1873 Map|publisher=David Rumsey|access-date=November 6, 2014}}</ref> The present 164th Street runs along the original border between the 4th and 6th districts of the town of Flushing.<ref name="Beers 1873 Map"/>

Adjacent neighborhoods include [[Forest Hills, Queens|Forest Hills]] to the west, [[Hillcrest, Queens|Hillcrest]] and [[Pomonok, Queens|Pomonok]] to the east, [[Briarwood, Queens|Briarwood]] to the south, and [[Queensboro Hill, Queens|Queensboro Hill]] to the north.

==History==

===Early settlement===
In the northwestern part of the neighborhood<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.scribd.com/doc/20770530/Willett-Family-History-Nov-2009-version-8-9|title= Willet Family History |page=18|publisher=Scribd.com|access-date=November 6, 2014}}</ref> was the location of the {{convert|120|acre|ha}} Spring Hill Farm.<ref name="Cedar Grove Playground">{{cite web|url=http://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/Q376/history |title=Cedar Grove Playground|publisher=Nycgovparks.gov|access-date=November 6, 2014}}</ref> The farm was part of the [[Francis Lewis]] estate during [[Colonial history of the United States|colonial]] times. By 1762 the farm was owned by Colonel Thomas Willet, High Sheriff of Flushing,<ref>''The History of the Several Towns, Manors, and Patents of the County of Westchester: From Its First Settlement to the Present Time'', Volume P.275 (Google eBook)</ref> and was sold to [[Cadwallader Colden]], lieutenant governor for the province of New York. In 1763 Colden built the Spring Hill House on the property. In 1783 the property was confiscated by the government because Cadwallader's son David was a [[Loyalist#North America|loyalist]] to the [[Monarchy of the United Kingdom|monarchy]]. By 1894 the Durkee family owned the property and sold it to the Cedar Grove Cemetery Corporation. The Spring Hill House became the office of the Cedar Grove Cemetery, until the house was later destroyed by a fire.<ref name="Cedar Grove Playground"/>

In the 19th century the area of Kew Gardens Hills was known as ''Head of the Fly'',<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.davidrumsey.com/luna/servlet/detail/RUMSEY~8~1~1770~190006:Map-Of-The-Country-Thirty-Three-Mil?sort=Pub_List_No_InitialSort%2CPub_Date%2CPub_List_No%2CSeries_No&qvq=sort:Pub_List_No_InitialSort%2CPub_Date%2CPub_List_No%2CSeries_No;lc:RUMSEY~8~1&mi=24&trs=31495|title= Colton 1853 Map of 33 Miles around NYC|publisher=Davidrumsey.com|access-date=November 6, 2014}}</ref> for its location at the headwaters of the Flushing Creek (or [[Flushing River]]). [[Vlaie|Fly]] or vly, being the Dutch word for swamp. One of the oldest roads through the area was called the Vleigh Road, and still exists today as Vleigh Place.<ref name="history">{{cite web|url=http://www.kghca.org/kewgardens.htm |title=Kew Gardens Hills: Articles pertaining to it and its history|author=Tina Morales|publisher=Kghca.org|access-date=May 23, 2012}}</ref>

Timothy Jackson operated a horse boarding stable near where the intersection of Park Drive East and Union Turnpike, or the [[Kew Gardens Interchange]] is today.<ref name="Beers 1873 Map"/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.davidrumsey.com/luna/servlet/detail/RUMSEY~8~1~217419~5503592:Kings-County-Business-Notices--Quee?sort=Pub_List_No_InitialSort%2CPub_Date%2CPub_List_No%2CSeries_No&qvq=q:long%2Bisland;sort:Pub_List_No_InitialSort%2CPub_Date%2CPub_List_No%2CSeries_No;lc:RUMSEY~8~1&mi=37&trs=206|title=Beers 1873 Queens County Business Notices|publisher=Davidrumsey.com|access-date=November 6, 2014}}</ref> On what is now the [[Jamaica Yard|Jamaica subway yard]] was previously a horse race course, built by Timothy Jackson, and was known as Whitepot Race & Track.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.queensnewyork.com/forest/buriedtreasure.html|title=Colonial House Of 1750 To Be Razed For New Parkway; Legend Says That General Hove Camped There In 1776.|publisher=Queensnewyork.com|access-date=November 6, 2014}}</ref> Although the train yard is not in [[Jamaica, Queens|Jamaica]], it is named Jamaica because the yard feeds the subway lines which begin (or end) in Jamaica. This area was an extension of Timothy Jackson's Willow Glen Farm for which the farmhouse was located south of Union Turnpike in the neighborhood of Jamaica that is now called [[Briarwood, Queens|Briarwood]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/Q212/highlights|title=NYC Park Department Queens Valley Playground|publisher=Nycgovparks.org|access-date=November 6, 2014}}</ref> In the 1750s, William Furman was the owner of the farm he named Willow Glen.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/Q212/highlights|title= NYC Parks: Queens Valley|publisher=Nycgovparks.org|access-date=November 6, 2014}}</ref> Today Willow Lake, at the southern end of [[Flushing Meadows–Corona Park]], retains the Willow name.

The municipal government of the Town of Flushing, which dated back to colonial times, along with other municipal township governments in [[Queens|Queens County]], was incorporated into the Borough of Queens on January 1, 1898. Later, the area, was named after [[Kew Gardens, Queens|Kew Gardens]], which in 1909 was renamed after [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]], in London, England.<ref name="nyt-namedfor"/>

The area's earliest modern homes were built in 1917 off Union Turnpike, but in the early 20th century, the area was known as Queens Valley and consisted mostly of farmland. By the 1920s many of the farms were sold to golf clubs or country clubs.<ref name="Kew Gardens Hills">{{cite web|url=http://www.longislandexchange.com/brooklynqueens/kewgardenshills.html|title=Kew Gardens Hills|publisher=Longislandexchange.com|access-date=July 5, 2009|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090315010923/http://www.longislandexchange.com/brooklynqueens/kewgardenshills.html|archive-date=March 15, 2009}}</ref> The golf courses that made up the area include the Spring Hill Golf Course, Queens Valley Golf Course, Pomonok Country Club, and Arrowbrook<ref>{{cite web|url=http://digitalgallery.nypl.org/nypldigital/dgkeysearchdetail.cfm?trg=1&strucID=1793504&imageID=1670911&word=golf%20club&s=1&notword=&d=&c=&f=&k=0&lWord=&lField=&sScope=&sLevel=&sLabel=&sort=&total=84&num=60&imgs=20&pNum=&pos=65|title= New York Public Library|publisher=Digitalgallery.nypl.org|access-date=June 11, 2012}}</ref> Country Club. In 1939, the Arrowbrook Country Club was the home of the "Summer City Hall" of Mayor La Guardia.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://fultonhistory.com/newspaper%2011/New%20York%20Evening%20Post/New%20York%20NY%20Evening%20Post%201939%20Grayscale/New%20York%20NY%20Evening%20Post%201939%20Grayscale%20-%200490.pdf|title=New York Evening Post|publisher=Fultonhistory.com|access-date=November 6, 2014}}</ref>

One road that ran through the area was called Quarrelsome Lane, which ran from Jamaica Road to Fresh Meadow Road; the road is now known as 75th Avenue. Jamaica Road, the most direct route between the villages of Flushing and Jamaica,<ref name="forgotten-ny.com">{{cite web|url=http://www.forgotten-ny.com/NEIGHBORHOODS/kg.hills/kghills.html |title=Forgotten NY Neighborhoods: Kew Gardens Hills|publisher=Forgotten-ny.com|access-date=July 5, 2009}}</ref> is now [[Kissena Boulevard]] and becomes [[Parsons Boulevard]] at the intersection of Quarrelsome Lane.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bklyn-genealogy-info.com/Map/Queens.1910.1.html|title=1910 Map of Queens|publisher=Bklyn-genealogy-info.com|access-date=November 6, 2014}}</ref>

===Later years===
[[File:Independencehallkgh.jpg|thumb|220px|left|Queens County Savings Bank on Main Street]]

Growth to Kew Gardens Hills came when [[Kew Gardens, Queens]], to the south, gained a [[IND Queens Boulevard Line|subway line]] at [[Queens Boulevard]] in 1936 and Flushing Meadows–Corona Park, directly to the northwest of the neighborhood, hosted the [[1939 New York World's Fair]]. Early residents were mostly German, Irish and Italian. Many were relocating from Brooklyn and Manhattan. The area was hilly and Kew Gardens was known as a prestigious Queens neighborhood and so developers changed its name from Queens Valley to Kew Gardens Hills.<ref name="nytimes.com">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2002/01/13/realestate/if-you-re-thinking-living-kew-gardens-hills-tranquil-enclave-especially-saturday.html|title= If You're Thinking of Living in Kew Gardens Hills; Tranquil Enclave, Especially on Saturday|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=January 13, 2002|access-date=July 5, 2009}}</ref>

The first Queen of Peace mass took place in 1939.<ref name=history /> Property along 144th Street, now part of Main Street, was seized by the city to complete the construction of Main Street from northern Flushing. Main Street was paved and bus routes began to serve the area in 1941. The Jewish Center of Kew Gardens Hills was established in 1941. The [[Queens County Savings Bank]] opened its branch in 1949 and local school, P.S. 164, also known as the Queens Valley School, also opened its doors that year.<ref>{{cite web|author=Gottlieb, Jeff |url=http://www.cqha.net/docs/Kew_Gardens_Hills_Five_The_v2.pdf |title=The Kew Gardens Hills Five |publisher=Queens Central Historical Association |access-date=July 5, 2009 }}{{dead link|date=December 2016 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

Main Street Cinemas—designed by architect Joseph Unger, who also designed the Trylon Theatre—opened in 1940 and operated by Interboro Circuit Inc. The 600 seat single screen theater was built at a cost of $75,000, and was dubbed one of the city's finest. The theater was later subdivided into a six screen cineplex and ultimately closed in September 2022.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Krichevsky |first=Sophie |date=September 8, 2022 |title=Main St. Cinemas closes its doors |url=https://www.qchron.com/editions/queenswide/main-st-cinemas-closes-its-doors/article_fceade86-c39c-5bad-8011-572bc6f69bb3.html |access-date=September 21, 2022 |website=Queens Chronicle}}</ref>

In 1941, Barney Spiegel bought a part of the [[Fresh Meadows, Queens#Klein Farm|Klein Farm]] at 69th Road and [[Main Street (Queens)|Main Street]].<ref name="tract">"[https://www.proquest.com/docview/106072085/869B4ECDA41422CPQ/9 Buys Old Farm Tract: Queens Builder Acquires Large Kew Gardens Property]". ''The New York Times''. April 20, 1941. p. RE4.</ref> On the land, he built 150 duplexes, designed by architect A. Salkowitz.<ref name= tract/>

On July 14, 1965, the neighborhood became infamous when five-year-old Eddie Crimmins Jr. and four-year-old Missy Crimmins vanished from their garden apartment at 150-22 72nd Drive. Missy's body was found the same day in a vacant lot on 71st Avenue at 162nd Street (the area where the 107th Precinct is located today.) Eddie's body was found five days later near 68th Drive and the entrance to the northbound Van Wyck Expressway. The children's mother, [[Alice Crimmins]], was convicted in 1971, and imprisoned, in the death of her children. She was paroled in 1977.<ref>[http://www.queenstribune.com/archives/anniversaryarchive/anniversary99/been_doin/tb_an_doin03.html]
* {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100302022500/http://www.queenstribune.com/archives/anniversaryarchive/anniversary99/been_doin/tb_an_doin03.html|date=March 2, 2010}}</ref>

On [[2010 Brooklyn/Queens tornadoes|September 16, 2010]], an [[Tornado|EF1 tornado]] touched down in [[Flushing Meadows–Corona Park]], causing widespread damage to cars and homes in the Kew Gardens Hills area. [[John Bowne High School]]—located along Main Street at the edge of the [[Queens College, City University of New York|CUNY Queens College]] campus, directly across from Mt. Hebron Cemetery—was the only New York City public school building to sustain physical damage related to the storm and was closed on the day after the storm.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/09/18/nyregion/18weather.html|title=City Workers Clear Debris in Aftermath of Fierce Storm|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=September 17, 2010 |access-date=November 6, 2014|last1=Barron |first1=James }}</ref>

==Demographics==
[[File:Haymsolomonkewgardenshills.jpg|thumb|220px|right|[[Haym Solomon]] Square in Kew Gardens Hills.]]
[[File:Queenofpeacekewgardenshills.jpg|thumb|220px|right|Queen of Peace Catholic Church in Kew Gardens Hills.]]
Based on data from the [[2010 United States census]], the population of Kew Gardens Hills was 37,479, an increase of 1,427 (4.0%) from the 36,052 counted in [[2000 United States census|2000]]. Covering an area of {{convert|873.05|acres}}, the neighborhood had a population density of {{convert|42.9|PD/acre|PD/sqmi PD/sqkm}}.<ref name="PLP5">[http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p5_nta.pdf Table PL-P5 NTA: Total Population and Persons Per Acre - New York City Neighborhood Tabulation Areas*, 2010], Population Division - [[New York City]] Department of City Planning, February 2012. Accessed June 16, 2016.</ref> The racial makeup of the neighborhood was 53.9% (20,184) [[White (U.S. Census)|White]], 7.6% (2,839) [[African American (U.S. Census)|African American]], 0.2% (63) [[Native American (U.S. Census)|Native American]], 20.0% (7,500) [[Asian (U.S. Census)|Asian]], 0.1% (20) [[Pacific Islander (U.S. Census)|Pacific Islander]], 0.4% (156) from [[Race (United States Census)|other races]], and 3.1% (1,169) from two or more races. [[Hispanic (U.S. Census)|Hispanic]] or [[Latino (U.S. Census)|Latino]] of any race were 14.8% (5,548) of the population.<ref name="PLP3A">[http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p3a_nta.pdf Table PL-P3A NTA: Total Population by Mutually Exclusive Race and Hispanic Origin - New York City Neighborhood Tabulation Areas*, 2010], Population Division - [[New York City]] Department of City Planning, March 29, 2011. Accessed June 14, 2016.</ref>

The entirety of Community Board 8, which comprises Kew Gardens Hills as well as [[Fresh Meadows, Queens|Fresh Meadows]] and [[Jamaica Hills, Queens|Jamaica Hills]], had 156,217 inhabitants as of [[New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene|NYC Health]]'s 2018 Community Health Profile, with an average life expectancy of 83.9 years.<ref name="CHP2018">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/data/2018chp-qn8.pdf|title=Hillcrest and Fresh Meadows (Including Briarwood, Fresh Meadows, Hillcrest, Jamaica Hills, Kew Gardens Hills and Utopia)|date=2018|website=nyc.gov|publisher=NYC Health|access-date=March 2, 2019}}</ref>{{Rp|2, 20}} This is higher than the median life expectancy of 81.2 for all New York City neighborhoods.<ref name=":21">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/tcny/community-health-assessment-plan.pdf|title=2016-2018 Community Health Assessment and Community Health Improvement Plan: Take Care New York 2020|date=2016|website=[[government of New York City|nyc.gov]]|publisher=[[New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene]]|access-date=September 8, 2017|archive-date=September 9, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170909004755/https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/tcny/community-health-assessment-plan.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>{{Rp|53 (PDF p. 84)}} Most inhabitants are middle-aged adults and youth: 20% are between the ages of 0–17, 28% between 25 and 44, and 27% between 45 and 64. The ratio of college-aged and elderly residents was lower, at 10% and 15% respectively.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|2}}

As of 2017, the median [[household income]] in Community Board 8 was $64,005.<ref name="CB8PUMA">{{cite web|url=https://censusreporter.org/profiles/79500US3604106-nyc-queens-community-district-8-briarwood-fresh-meadows-hillcrest-puma-ny/|title=NYC-Queens Community District 8--Briarwood, Fresh Meadows & Hillcrest PUMA, NY|publisher=Census Reporter|access-date=July 17, 2018|archive-date=March 8, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190308080836/https://censusreporter.org/profiles/79500US3604106-nyc-queens-community-district-8-briarwood-fresh-meadows-hillcrest-puma-ny/|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 2018, an estimated 22% of Kew Gardens Hills residents lived in poverty, compared to 19% in all of Queens and 20% in all of New York City. One in eleven residents (9%) were unemployed, compared to 8% in Queens and 9% in New York City. Rent burden, or the percentage of residents who have difficulty paying their rent, is 54% in Kew Gardens Hills, slightly higher than the boroughwide and citywide rates of 53% and 51% respectively. Based on this calculation, {{as of|2018|lc=y}}, Kew Gardens Hills is considered to be high-income relative to the rest of the city and not [[gentrification|gentrifying]].<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|7}} The neighborhood has been described as "a largely [[middle class|middle-class]] area".<ref>Warshawer, Gabby. [https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424052702303448204579339450498877752 "Kew Gardens Hills Has an Identity All Its Own Neighborhood in Central Queens Has Suburban Feel, Manageable Commutes"], ''[[Wall Street Journal]]'', January 24, 2014. Accessed November 14, 2020. "Residents of Kew Gardens Hills, in central Queens, say the area's appeals include its suburban feel and manageable commutes made possible by its proximity to several highways. The neighborhood, which is distinct from nearby Kew Gardens, is a largely middle-class area that was originally part of Flushing and called Queens Valley in the early part of the 20th century."</ref>

The neighborhood contains an established [[Jew]]ish population, some [[Israeli Americans|Israelis]] and [[Bukharan Jews]], as well as smaller groups of [[Latinos]], [[Koreans]], [[Han Chinese|Chinese]], [[India]]ns, [[Afghanistan|Afghans]] and [[African American]]s. Kew Gardens Hills is home to the largest concentration of [[Afghanistan|Afghanis]] in the New York metropolitan area.<ref name="bcny">{{cite web|url=http://www.bcnychurchplanting.org/uploaded_files/Afghan%20Muslim%20Profile.pdf|title=All Peoples Initiative|publisher=Bcnychurchplanting.org|access-date=June 12, 2012|url-status=usurped|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131203053803/http://www.bcnychurchplanting.org/uploaded_files/Afghan%20Muslim%20Profile.pdf|archive-date=December 3, 2013}}</ref>


==Religious communities==
The local Jewish community contains an established [[Orthodox Judaism|Orthodox]] [[Jew]]ish population and some [[Israeli Americans|Israelis]] and [[Bukharan Jews]].<ref name="bcny"/> There are several dozen houses of worship in Kew Gardens Hills, many of them Jewish. Established in 1941, the Jewish Center of Kew Gardens Hills is the only traditional Conservative synagogue located in the heart of Kew Gardens Hills. By the 1950s, the [[Orthodox Jewish]] community began to take root.

[[File:Yeshiva_Keser_Torah,_minyan_factory_in_Kew_Gardens_Hill,_May_2020.jpg|thumb|right|Yeshiva Keser Torah]]

The first orthodox Jewish synagogue was formed in 1950 on Parsons Boulevard and 78th Road when the Jewish Center of Torath Emeth was formed with Rabbi Joel Laks as the spiritual leader. The following year, the [[National Council of Young Israel|Young Israel]] Congregation of Kew Gardens Hills was founded in 1951 with 15 families. That congregation now consists of 450 families.<ref>Halapid, Official Publication of YIKGH November–December 2010 Issue p.23-27</ref> Congregation Machzikei Hadas formed by Rabbi Yosef Gelernter on 73rd Avenue, is home to the first [[mikveh]] in Kew Gardens Hills.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Kew Gardens Hills, Queens (History) – UrbanAreas.net|url=https://urbanareas.net/info/resources/neighborhoods-queens/kew-gardens-hills-queens-history/|access-date=2022-01-19|website=urbanareas.net}}</ref> In March 1960, the City Council named a small park at Vleigh Place and Main Street as Freedom Square to commemorate the one hundredth anniversary of the birth of [[Theodor Herzl]], founder of present-day Zionism.<ref name="forgotten-ny.com"/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/freedom-square-playground|title=Freedom Square Playground Map : NYC Parks|website=www.nycgovparks.org}}</ref> The Yeshivas [[Yeshivas Chofetz Chaim|Chafetz Chaim]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.duvys.com/simple/rsa|title = RSA Donation Page}}</ref> [[Yeshivas Ohr HaChaim|Ohr Hachaim]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.godaven.com/shul-details/603|title = Godaven | Yeshiva Ohr Hachaim}}</ref> and [[Yeshiva Kesser Torah|Kesser Torah]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.theyeshivaworld.com/news/boruch-dayan-emmes/1703332/levaya-of-harav-elyakim-rosenblatt-zatzal-rosh-yeshiva-of-kesser-torah-in-queens.html|title = Levaya of HaRav Elyakim Rosenblatt ZATZAL, Rosh Yeshiva of Kesser Torah in Queens|date = March 28, 2019}}</ref> are situated in Kew Gardens Hills. Jewish elementary schools include [[Yeshiva Ketana of Queens]]<ref>{{Cite web|title=Home|url=https://yeshivaketana.com/|access-date=2022-01-19|website=yeshivaketana.com|language=en-US}}</ref> and Yeshiva of Central Queens.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Yeshiva of Central Queens|url=https://ycqweb.com/|access-date=2022-01-19}}</ref>

Other houses of worship include the Roman Catholic Church Queen of Peace, located on Main Street at 77th Road. St. Nicholas of Tolentine is located on Parsons Boulevard behind east of Parkway Village. The Lutheran Church of the Ascension is located on Main Street just south of Union Turnpike. The Lutheran Church of the Redeemer, located on 65th Avenue near Parsons Boulevard, is also the facility used by the Korean Grace Community Church.

A sizable [[Muslim]] and [[Sikh]] population exists, most notably on the northern side with several stores catering to that population.

== Health ==
{{As of|2018}}, [[preterm birth]]s and births to teenage mothers are less common in Kew Gardens Hills than in other places citywide. In Kew Gardens Hills, there were 74 preterm births per 1,000 live births (compared to 87 per 1,000 citywide), and 6.7 births to teenage mothers per 1,000 live births (compared to 19.3 per 1,000 citywide).<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|11}} Kew Gardens Hills has a relatively average population of residents who are [[Health insurance coverage in the United States|uninsured]]. In 2018, this population of uninsured residents was estimated to be 11%, which is slightly lower than the citywide rate of 12%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|14}}

The concentration of [[particulates|fine particulate matter]], the deadliest type of [[air pollution|air pollutant]], in Kew Gardens Hills is {{convert|0.0078|mg/m3|oz/ft3}}, lower than the citywide and boroughwide averages.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|9}} Fourteen percent of Kew Gardens Hills residents are [[Smoking|smokers]], which is equal to the city average of 14% of residents being smokers.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|13}} In Kew Gardens Hills, 19% of residents are [[Obesity|obese]], 11% are [[Diabetes mellitus|diabetic]], and 29% have [[hypertension|high blood pressure]]—compared to the citywide averages of 20%, 14%, and 24% respectively.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|16}} In addition, 18% of children are obese, compared to the citywide average of 20%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|12}}

Eighty-nine percent of residents eat some fruits and vegetables every day, which is higher than the city's average of 87%. In 2018, 79% of residents described their health as "good", "very good", or "excellent", about the same as the city's average of 78%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|13}} For every supermarket in Kew Gardens Hills, there are 5 [[convenience store|bodegas]].<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|10}}

The nearest large hospitals to Kew Gardens Hills are the [[Queens Hospital Center]] in Jamaica and [[NewYork–Presbyterian/Queens]] in Flushing.<ref>{{cite web | last=Finkel | first=Beth | title=Guide To Queens Hospitals | website=Queens Tribune | date=February 27, 2014 | url=http://queenstribune.com/guide-to-queens-hospitals/ | access-date=March 7, 2019 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170204185507/http://queenstribune.com/guide-to-queens-hospitals/ | archive-date=February 4, 2017 | url-status=dead }}</ref>

===Co-named streets===
[[File:Rabbi_H_Joel_Laks_Way.jpg|thumb|upright|Dr. Rabbi H. Joel Laks Way, at the corner of the street his synagogue was on]] 
Because of the large Jewish population in Kew Gardens Hills, six streets in the neighborhood were named or co-named after notable Jews:
*Freedom Square, named in honor of [[Theodor Herzl]]'s quest for a Jewish homeland
*Rabbi Kirshblum Triangle, named for the first Rabbi of the Kew Gardens Hills Jewish Center
*Dr. Rabbi H. Joel Laks Way on 78th Road between Parsons Boulevard and 160 Street, named for the founder of the first orthodox synagogue in the area
*Rabbi Avraham Schechter Way, named for a prominent resident of the community is located between 147th Street and 150th Street along 72nd Drive
*[[Haym Salomon]] Square (geometrically a triangle), across from the Kew Gardens Hills branch of the [[Queens Borough Public Library]], named for the Revolutionary War financier
*Abe Wolfson Triangle, named for an environmental activist and one of the founders of the Queens Historical Society, is located along Kissena Boulevard near 75th Avenue.

==Structures==
[[File:Gardenaptkewgardenshills.jpg|thumb|220px|right|Regency Gardens, one of many Kew Gardens Hills garden apartments]]
[[File:Outsidepark apt150-20.JPG|220px|right|thumb|The intersection of 71st Avenue and 150th Street in eastern Kew Gardens Hills]]

Kew Gardens Hills is a mixed neighborhood of single-family homes – detached or in rows – as well as three to six-story garden apartment buildings mostly built during the years immediately following [[World War II]], such as Regency Gardens. These apartments are characterized by their lawns and internal pathways that give the complexes a small-neighborhood feel. There are several homes in Kew Gardens Hills that predate Main Street, whose property was subject to eminent domain in the 1930s to widen 144th Street into the Main Street extension from northern Flushing. A few public [[housing projects]] in one part of the neighborhood were also built. Other buildings in that area were built to house employees of certain unions, including the [[Electchester, Queens|Electchester]] Co-operative Building, built for electrical employees in 1949 on what used to be the grounds of the [[Pomonok Country Club]], which no longer houses electrical employees exclusively.<ref name="forgotten-ny.com"/>

A pedestrian entrance is located on Main Street near Gravett Road. [[Cedar Grove Cemetery (Queens, New York)|Cedar Grove Cemetery]] was founded in 1894 as a [[Nonsectarian|non-sectarian]] [[cemetery]]. *[https://web.archive.org/web/20120530080727/http://www.mounthebroncemetery.com/ Mount Hebron Cemetery] uses the same roads as Cedar Grove cemetery but since 1909 has operated independently as a [[Jewish cemetery]]. As of 2012, over 217,000 burials have taken place at Mount Hebron.

Here, members of the Willet and Colden families, former owners of the property, are said to have been laid to rest. The [[Headstone|stone]] of Elizabeth Willet, dated October 19, 1773 is still standing. Another stone dated 1722 is partially covered but visible.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://nycemetery.wordpress.com/2011/04/28/willett-family-burial-ground/|title=Willett Family Burial Ground|work=New York City Cemetery Project|access-date=November 6, 2014|date=April 28, 2011}}</ref>

This private family cemetery was established in 1853, but the land was sold by Troy's descendants in 1915.
